Social science works with an "anthropocentric" picture on which the social world is built out of people, as an ant colony is built out of ants. Part Two argues that even facts about groups, including group action and intention, are grounded in more than the members. Part Two argues that facts about groups, including their actions and intentions, are grounded in more than their members, which bears directly on [THEORY-043](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-043.md). The planning structures that organise an individual's agency over time are also at the core of small-scale shared agency. | [LIT-684](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-684.md) v4 | Responsibility and Control: A Theory of Moral Responsibility | Fischer & Ravizza (1998), Cambridge University Press. Unread seed. The most influential reasons-responsiveness theory of moral responsibility. Responsibility requires guidance control, not regulative control (the control that involves alternative possibilities), and Frankfurt-type cases show the two come apart. An agent has guidance control of an action when it issues from her own, moderately reasons-responsive mechanism: regularly receptive to reasons, including moral ones, and at least weakly reactive to them. The mechanism is her own when she has taken responsibility for it, which makes responsibility historical. Guidance control so described is compatible with causal determinism, which is the position Fischer calls semicompatibilism. | Unavailable — registered 2026-10-03 as a seed, from Crossref's book and chapter records, the chapter openings Cambridge Core displays, the record's second-hand readings, the SEP entry Moral Responsibility ([LIT-691](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-691.md)) and Fischer's own summary in "Stories and the Meaning of Life" ([LIT-689](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-689.md), read), not read.
